nameStory: This shrub gets its name from two key clues: it loves boggy, wet places, and it was first scientifically described from specimens found in Labrador. Indigenous peoples across northern North America have long brewed its leaves into medicinal teas, earning it names like Hudson's Bay tea and muskeg tea.
description: Bog Labrador tea is a low-growing evergreen shrub that typically reaches 2-4 feet tall, forming dense patches in wet, acidic areas. It has distinctive leathery leaves that are dark green on top and rusty-brown fuzzy underneath, giving it a two-toned appearance. In late spring to early summer, it produces clusters of small white flowers that look like tiny stars. This hardy northern shrub thrives in some of New England's most challenging environments.

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Narrow, leathery evergreen leaves with rolled edges that feel thick and waxy. The undersides are covered in dense rusty-brown or orange fuzzy hairs that you can easily see and feel - this rusty fuzz is the plant's signature feature.

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Small white flowers with 5 petals arranged in rounded clusters at branch tips. Each flower is about half an inch across with prominent stamens that stick out like tiny pins. Blooms smell faintly sweet.

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Forms low, spreading colonies of upright stems rarely taller than 4 feet. Branches are slender and somewhat woody, often leaning or arching outward from the center of the clump.

idTips.label: Bark
idTips.description: Young stems are smooth and reddish-brown, while older stems develop thin, peeling bark. The wood feels brittle and breaks with a clean snap when bent.

idTips.label: Fruit/Seeds
idTips.description: Produces small, dry capsules that split open to release tiny seeds. The capsules are light brown and remain on the plant through winter, often still visible when new flowers appear.

habitat: Look for bog Labrador tea in New England's coldest, wettest spots - sphagnum bogs, wet meadows, swampy areas, and the edges of ponds and streams. It thrives in acidic, nutrient-poor soils and is often found growing alongside cranberries, pitcher plants, and other bog specialists. Most common in northern New England, especially in higher elevations and areas with cooler climates.

seasonality.spring: New growth emerges as bright green shoots, and flower buds begin to swell. The contrast between old dark leaves and fresh growth is quite noticeable.
seasonality.summer: Peak blooming occurs from late May through July, with clusters of white flowers attracting bees and other pollinators. This is the best time for positive identification.
seasonality.fall: Flowers fade and seed capsules develop. Leaves may take on slightly more bronze tones but remain evergreen.
seasonality.winter: Evergreen leaves persist but may curl more tightly. The rusty-fuzzy leaf undersides become even more apparent as a key identification feature when other bog plants have died back.

funFact: The fuzzy brown hairs on the leaf undersides aren't just for show - they're actually a clever adaptation that helps the plant survive harsh bog conditions by reducing water loss and protecting against cold winds, essentially giving each leaf its own tiny fur coat!
confusionNotes: Most likely confused with other bog shrubs like leatherleaf or bog rosemary, but neither of those has the distinctive rusty-fuzzy leaf undersides. Memory trick: 'Labrador' dogs have fuzzy coats, and Labrador tea has fuzzy leaf undersides.
contextualKnowledge: This plant was historically important to northern indigenous peoples and early settlers as a tea substitute, but modern foragers should be cautious - while traditional preparation methods made it safe, the raw leaves contain compounds that can be harmful if consumed improperly.
compareHints: Unlike its showy rhododendron and azalea cousins with their large, colorful flowers, bog Labrador tea has small white blooms and much narrower leaves. While other rhododendrons prefer well-drained woodland soils, this species is uniquely adapted to waterlogged, acidic bog conditions. Its evergreen nature also sets it apart from most New England azaleas, which are deciduous.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Unlike other rhododendrons and azaleas in New England, rhodora has distinctly irregular flowers with 3 upper lobes and 2 lower petals, rather than the typical 5-petaled funnel shape.
Great rhododendron dwarfs other native rhododendrons and azaleas in New England with its massive size and evergreen leaves - most others are deciduous shrubs under 8 feet tall.
Among New England's native azaleas, swamp azalea is unique for its white flowers and wet habitat preferences - pinxter flower and early azalea both have pink flowers and prefer drier sites.

Unlike its tall cousins like Great Rhododendron or the various azaleas found in New England's lowlands, Lapland Azalea is dramatically smaller and adapted for arctic conditions rather than woodland understories.
Early azalea differs from other native azaleas by its serrated leaf edges and early bloom time.
Among New England's native azaleas, pinxter flower is distinguished by its pink color and early bloom time before leaf emergence.
Unlike the evergreen great rhododendron with its large leathery leaves and white flowers, flame azalea loses its leaves in winter and produces much more intensely colored blooms.

Among New England's rhododendrons and azaleas, pinkshell azalea stands out for its soft pink, shell-like flowers and graceful, open growth habit - most other azaleas are either denser in form or have different flower colors and textures.
Among New England's rhododendrons and azaleas, Catawba rhododendron is distinguished by its purple flowers and evergreen leaves.
Among New England rhododendrons, Carolina rhododendron stands out for its small, compact size and late spring bloom time.
Unlike our native azaleas which tend to have pink, white, or orange flowers, red azalea stands out with its intense red blooms.
